questions.scenario: After nine months of Claude Code adoption across 180 engineers, a platform team reports that pull request cycle time has improved and that two junior engineers have been promoted. The same team also reports that 22% of AI-assisted pull requests needed a second pass for test coverage, and that on-call pages in one service have roughly doubled.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible reading of this evidence?

options.text: Delivery metrics improved and quality signals did not, so the honest conclusion is partial: throughput gains alongside a review burden and an operational cost that need to be measured on their own terms.
The promotion evidence shows the change worked, so the coverage and on-call numbers are noise from a small number of services.
The on-call increase shows the change failed, so the throughput and promotion results should be discounted.
No conclusion is available without a controlled comparison group, since observational metrics cannot be attributed to the tooling.

questions.explanation: The four signals measure different things and they do not agree, so the defensible position is that **some outcomes improved and others need attention**. Throughput and promotion are real evidence of value; the coverage gap and the doubled on-call load are real evidence of cost. Neither cancels the other, and each points at a specific remedy — review capacity and test conventions for the first, observability for the second. Waiting for a control group is a research standard, not a prerequisite for acting on a measurable regression.

whyWrong.B: Two promotions are not a controlled measure of tooling impact and cannot outweigh 22% of pull requests needing rework. Treating inconvenient metrics as noise is the failure mode of an adoption review.
whyWrong.C: A doubling of on-call pages in one service is a serious signal, but it does not invalidate throughput gains elsewhere. Discarding the positive results because of one regression loses the ability to act on both.
whyWrong.D: A control group is the strongest form of evidence and is rarely available at this scale. The numbers here are sufficient to justify investigating the on-call increase, and too clear to ignore while waiting for certainty.

questions.mindset: When delivery and quality signals disagree, report both and name the remedy each points at — do not resolve the tension by discounting one.

questions.scenario: An organisation has tracked four metrics for its AI-assisted pipeline: pull requests merged, review comments per pull request, escaped defects, and mean time to restore. Pull requests merged rose 40%. The other three were flat.
questions.stem: What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: Throughput improved without an observable change in review load or defect rate, which is consistent with genuine productivity gain rather than work being pushed downstream.
Review load and defect rate rarely move, so the flat figures should not be read as meaningful.
The merged count is the wrong metric entirely and should be replaced before any further decisions are made.
Flat defect rates alongside rising throughput indicate that the extra work is of lower quality, whatever review load shows.

questions.explanation: Raised throughput with **flat quality and review load** is the pattern you would want to see. If generated code were pushing work downstream, review comments per pull request would rise as reviewers absorb more, and escaped defects would rise as more code reached production per period. Both flat means the additional throughput was absorbed without additional human cost. One caveat is honest: merged count and escaped defects measure volume and outcomes, not whether the change is right — that is what lead time for changes and time to restore cover.

whyWrong.B: Flat review load and flat defects are exactly the observations that make the throughput figure interpretable. They are the control signals that show the gain was not bought with downstream cost.
whyWrong.C: Merged count is one of the four DORA measures and is worth keeping, because it is the clearest evidence that something changed. Replacing it before investigating why three other measures did not move would discard the finding.
whyWrong.D: If quality had degraded, escaped defects would rise rather than stay flat. Flat defects with rising volume is the opposite pattern, and it is what makes the improvement credible.

questions.mindset: Throughput gains only count when review load and defects stay flat — those flat signals are what show the work was not pushed downstream.

questions.scenario: A leader asks whether AI-assisted development is 'making developers faster'. The team has measured that a task the team previously took four hours now takes three, and that developers also spend about forty minutes a day reviewing and correcting generated changes.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful measurement change?

options.text: Separate gross task speed from the review and correction time it creates, and measure both per unit of work delivered — otherwise the saving is offset by work the metric does not see.
Keep measuring task duration only, since review time is a fixed overhead that will fall as developers get better at prompting.
Move to measuring lines of code produced, since it is the most objective available proxy for output.
Survey developer satisfaction instead, since experienced judgement about their own productivity is the most reliable signal available.

questions.explanation: The headline figure and the correction time are **the same change measured from two ends**, and only reporting one end gives a false answer. Three hours of task time with forty minutes of daily review is not a 25% saving — it is closer to break-even, and could be negative on complex work. Measuring gross speed and the review it generates together is what makes the comparison honest, and it also points at the thing worth optimising: fewer changes needing correction.

whyWrong.B: This asserts that review time will fall without evidence, and it is the metric doing the damage. If review time rises instead, the organisation is making the accounting mistake it was trying to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Lines of code rewards volume, which is precisely the wrong thing when the question is whether work is getting done correctly and sustainably. It would show a large gain under either scenario.
whyWrong.D: Developer perception is worth asking about and is not a substitute for measurement. Practitioners are good at saying whether work feels better and poor at quantifying the offsetting time they now spend elsewhere.

questions.mindset: If tooling creates review work, both must be on the same axis or the saving is measured without its cost.

questions.scenario: A company is rolling Claude Code out to 400 engineers across 40 repositories. It has one CLAUDE.md, one settings file and no distribution mechanism. An enablement team has four weeks before the first wave.
questions.stem: Which TWO steps would MOST improve the rollout? Choose TWO.

options.text: Publish a shared baseline that every repository inherits — a common configuration and instruction file managed centrally, so the 40 repositories do not each invent their own.
Build a pilot with 8-10 engineers from different stacks, using real work, and use what breaks to revise the shared configuration before the first wave.
Enable every permission that exists, so engineers are not blocked, and tighten anything that causes problems later.
Write the rollout guidance from the enablement team's own experience, and publish it before any pilot so everyone has a reference.

questions.explanation: Two structural choices make this work at 400 engineers. A **shared baseline that repositories inherit** means conventions, permissions and security settings are consistent and centrally revised, rather than 40 local variations that diverge within a quarter. And a **pilot on real work by people from different stacks** is the only thing that surfaces what the shared configuration gets wrong — permission prompts that are too frequent, instructions that conflict with an existing repository — before it reaches 400 people.

whyWrong.C: Wide permissions remove friction and remove the guardrails together. Security teams will not approve it, and the first genuinely destructive action becomes the thing that ends the rollout.
whyWrong.D: Guidance written from theory goes out and gets corrected in practice, which is a slower way to learn than a pilot. Its authors will not have hit the repository-specific problems that only surface on real work.

questions.mindset: Rollouts at scale need a centrally inherited baseline and a pilot that finds what it gets wrong before the first wave.

questions.scenario: An engineering organisation is standardising Claude Code across teams and has found that each team's project instructions are a different shape: one is 200 lines with historical rules, one is three words, one mixes conventions with a release process. Engineers moving between teams get inconsistent behaviour and ask enablement for help.
questions.stem: What is the BEST way to standardise team conventions?

options.text: Define a short shared skeleton for project instructions — what must be in them, in what order, and a length guidance — and let each team fill in its own specifics, with the shared parts genuinely shared.
Publish one organisation-wide instruction file, so every team behaves identically regardless of what it works on.
Give each team a copy of a reference example and let them decide how much of it to adopt.
Leave the instructions alone, since the teams' conventions are genuinely different and standardising them would flatten useful difference.

questions.explanation: The problem is not that conventions differ — they legitimately do — it is that **the file's role is unclear in each repository**. A shared skeleton makes the parts that must be the same the same: where conventions live, where the build and test commands are, what a generated change must do before being called done. What follows is genuinely team-specific. That gives an engineer moving teams a predictable place to look, without pretending a payments service and a design system share conventions.

whyWrong.B: An organisation-wide instruction file cannot contain 40 teams' real conventions, and what it does contain will be wrong for most of them. Conformity to a generic file is not the standardisation that helps.
whyWrong.C: An example without a specified structure reproduces exactly the inconsistency being complained about. Two teams reading the same reference will produce two different shapes.
whyWrong.D: There is real difference here, and it is why the shared parts are small. The complaint is about not knowing where to look, which a skeleton fixes without removing the difference.

questions.mindset: Standardise the shape and the shared content, not the conventions themselves — a skeleton makes the file's role predictable without flattening real differences.

questions.scenario: A company has decided to move one team onto an agentic workflow in which the agent plans, writes code, runs tests and opens a pull request. The team has no CI configuration, no test suite, and no code review requirements for agent-generated changes.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate advice?

options.text: Do not move this team yet. An agent that can open pull requests needs the verification the missing CI and tests would provide; without them the agent's own report is the only evidence the change is correct.
Move the team and require an engineer to approve every pull request, which provides the verification the missing CI would have.
Move the team but keep the agent's ability to open pull requests disabled until the test suite exists, so it still plans and writes code.
Move the team, and treat test coverage and CI as a follow-up, since the agent will add tests as part of its work.

questions.explanation: The prerequisites are not about agent capability, they are about **whether anything can check the work**. If the agent can open pull requests in a repository with no CI and no tests, then 'done' means the agent said so — the same unverifiable signal that produced every confident-but-wrong change the bank warns about. Building the verification first is the sequence that makes an agentic workflow safe, and on this team it is also the prerequisite that makes the agent useful rather than merely fast.

whyWrong.B: A human approving every pull request is verification, but it is the most expensive form and it scales badly — which defeats the point of the workflow. It also leaves the human doing by eye what a test suite should be doing automatically.
whyWrong.C: This is a defensible intermediate step and it is not what was proposed. It reduces the agent to a code-suggestion tool, so the organisation would be evaluating the wrong workflow when it decides whether agentic works here.
whyWrong.D: Assuming the agent will add the tests inverts the dependency. Tests written by the same agent that wrote the code, with nothing to check them, do not provide the independent verification the change needs.

questions.mindset: An agent that opens pull requests needs CI and tests first — otherwise its own report is the only evidence anything is correct.

questions.scenario: Two teams ran a six-week trial of AI-assisted development. Team A runs a mature service with a strong test suite and a two-reviewer rule. Team B runs a legacy service with no tests and one reviewer. Team A reports a clear gain. Team B reports no gain and higher review burden.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible conclusion for the organisation?

options.text: The difference is explained by verification maturity, not by the teams or the tooling. Team B's result is what absence of tests predicts, and the prerequisite is a test suite rather than a different adoption strategy.
Team B should be given more time, since six weeks is not enough to see an effect on a codebase of that size.
Team A's result should not be generalised to other teams, because six weeks is too short to establish any conclusion.
The difference is most likely the reviewers' experience, so Team B should pair with Team A's reviewers for the next trial.

questions.explanation: The two results differ along a dimension that explains them: **whether anything can independently verify a generated change**. Team A has a test suite and two reviewers, so generated code arrives already checkable and the gain is available. Team B has neither, so every change is unverifiable and review becomes the bottleneck — which is exactly the burden they reported. That points at a specific prerequisite rather than at patience or a change of reviewers.

whyWrong.B: More time on the same footing produces the same structure: without a test suite there is no way for a gain to show up in delivery, because the review step absorbs it regardless of how long the trial runs.
whyWrong.C: The caution is right about generalising and wrong about the evidence. The comparison is informative precisely because two teams under the same tooling produced different results for a reason the data identifies.
whyWrong.D: Reviewer experience is part of Team A's position but not the variable that distinguishes the teams. Moving reviewers to Team B raises the cost of each change without creating the automated verification that produced Team A's gain.

questions.mindset: When two teams get different results from the same tooling, look for the structural difference — verification maturity explains gains that review load alone does not.

questions.scenario: A company wants to know whether an expensive AI-assisted pipeline is working. Its dashboard shows tokens consumed, sessions started, lines changed and self-reported satisfaction. A colleague notes that none of these would reveal that generated changes are being reverted a week after merge.
questions.stem: Which TWO additions would MOST improve the dashboard? Choose TWO.

options.text: Track the rate at which merged changes are subsequently reverted or hot-fixed, which is where downstream cost shows up.
Track time from first commit to production for changes produced with assistance against those produced without, on the same service.
Track satisfaction scores more frequently, since sentiment is the earliest signal of a problem.
Track tokens per merged change, since efficiency per unit of output is the clearest measure of value.

questions.explanation: Both additions measure things the current four cannot: **where bad work is discovered** (reverts and hot fixes, which surface the quality cost that lines-changed hides) and **whether the whole cycle actually got shorter** (lead time to production on the same service, which includes the review and fix-up work the dashboard omits). Together they convert the dashboard from a usage report into an outcome report. Tokens and session counts stay useful for cost attribution, but they are inputs.

whyWrong.C: Satisfaction is a lagging and heavily conditioned signal. People report on how a tool feels, not on whether the code they merged was correct a fortnight later.
whyWrong.D: Tokens per change measures efficiency of consumption, not value delivered. A change can be expensive, small and wrong, or cheap, large and correct, and this ratio cannot tell those apart.

questions.mindset: A usage dashboard cannot answer whether the pipeline works — measure where defects surface and whether the whole cycle got shorter.

questions.scenario: A new team is adopting Claude Code. Their CLAUDE.md is empty, their build takes 25 minutes locally, and they have told the agent nothing about how their service is structured. Their first week of use has been dominated by timeouts and by suggestions that ignore their conventions.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST improve their first week? Choose TWO.

options.text: Record in the project instructions how to build, test and run the service, and the conventions that a change is expected to follow.
Give the agent the fastest available feedback loop — a targeted test command rather than the full suite — and tell it which command that is.
Add every internal service name and every historical design decision to the instructions, so nothing is missing.
Turn on extended thinking and the most capable model, so the agent reasons more carefully about the codebase.

questions.explanation: Both symptoms have a **missing input** as their cause. The agent has not been told how to verify its own work, so a 25-minute full-suite run is what it reaches for, which is why it times out; the agent has not been told the conventions, which is why it proposes things the team does not accept. Telling it the fast, targeted command is a small instruction with an outsized effect on throughput in the first week.

whyWrong.C: Loading historical decisions and every service name does not help with a missing build-and-test command and makes the instructions longer to read for everyone, including the agent. More context is not the answer to a missing specific.
whyWrong.D: A stronger model with more careful reasoning still does not know the team's conventions or how their tests run. This is a case where capability is not the binding constraint.

questions.mindset: When a team has timeouts and off-convention suggestions, the cause is unstated knowledge — the build command and the conventions, not the model.

questions.scenario: A platform team has written a PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter on every file the agent edits. Formatting failures were arriving in CI about one pull request in five. The hook exists and has been firing. Two engineers report the same recent failures.
questions.stem: Which TWO responses are well founded? Choose TWO.

options.text: Check the hook's matcher covers every path that can change a file, since edits made outside it — a different write tool, an already-staged file, a change from a script — reach CI unformatted.
Put a formatter run and the test command in the normal pull request checks, so whatever path the change came through is caught before merge.
Investigate whether the hook is running too slowly, since CI is receiving files before formatting completes.
Add a line to the project instructions telling the agent never to make an unformatted edit, since the instruction will cover the paths the hook does not match.

questions.explanation: A hook covers **the calls its matcher is configured to match**, and a residual one-in-five failure rate is the signature of write paths outside it. So there are two responses and they do different jobs. **Closing the matcher gap** removes the cause for the paths the hook does not cover. **Verifying in CI** catches anything that slips through regardless of which path produced it — including the ones that never run locally, such as container builds and generated files. Together they make the check independent of how the edit was made.

whyWrong.C: Hook latency would affect everything the hook touches, not one pull request in five. A consistently slow hook produces consistent failures, in the developer's working copy as well as CI.
whyWrong.D: An instruction is a request, and the gap is structural: files changed outside the matched tool calls will not be caught by a line of text about behaviour. This is the case where the hook is the control, not the instruction.

questions.mindset: Close the matcher gap and verify in CI — the hook covers the calls it matches, and CI catches everything else.

questions.scenario: A payments team keeps card-data handling rules in a directory-scoped CLAUDE.md. Engineers launch Claude Code from the repository root, which is how their tooling is configured. Security has confirmed that loading the rules depends on the working directory.
questions.stem: What is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Put the rules where they load regardless of where the session starts — the project-level instructions — and keep the directory-scoped file for detail that is only relevant inside that service.
Add an instruction to the root CLAUDE.md telling the agent to read the payments directory's CLAUDE.md before working in that service.
Ask engineers to start sessions from inside the service directory and record it as an onboarding step, since the current configuration is working.
Add the card-data rules to the organisation-wide managed settings, so every team receives them automatically.

questions.explanation: A control that only loads in some working directories is a control that is absent in the others, and here that means the session where card-data rules most need to be in view. Moving them to the instructions that load from the repository root makes the rule **reliably present regardless of how the session was started**, while the directory-scoped file keeps the detail where it belongs. That is the difference between a convention and a control.

whyWrong.B: An instruction to read another file makes the agent decide whether to, every time, on every session. That is a request, not a guarantee, and security asked for a control.
whyWrong.C: This accepts a control that silently does not apply. Engineers start sessions wherever their tooling defaults to, and an onboarding step cannot be relied on for a compliance rule — nor does it hold for automated and CI contexts.
whyWrong.D: Managed settings distribute rules to people who do not work on payments. Card-handling rules in an organisation-wide file would be read constantly by teams with no payment context and would not be targeted where they are needed.

questions.mindset: A control that only loads in some working directories is a control that is absent in the others — put compliance rules where they always load.

questions.scenario: A company runs a nightly Claude Code pipeline that reformats files, runs tests, and opens pull requests for anything that changed. It failed silently for a week: pull requests stopped appearing and nobody noticed until a release went out with an unformatted file and a failing test in it.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST improve this pipeline's reliability? Choose TWO.

options.text: Make the job report success or failure to a place a human or an alerting system sees, so silence is never the signal.
Break the job into steps with an explicit pass or fail after each, and fail the run rather than continuing, so a partial failure cannot look like success.
Add a formatting check and the test command to the normal pull request checks, so the pipeline's output is verified independently of the pipeline itself.
Schedule the pipeline to run twice as often, so a silent failure is discovered sooner.

questions.explanation: The failure mode is that **silence and success look the same**, and the two changes address that directly. Reporting the outcome somewhere visible makes an unrun or failed job announce itself. Breaking the job into steps with an explicit check after each means a partial failure stops the run instead of producing output that looks complete. Together they convert a pipeline that fails quietly into one that fails loudly.

whyWrong.C: This is worth doing and it does not address the failure described. It would have caught this particular bad release earlier, but the pipeline would still have been silently broken the following week.
whyWrong.D: Running twice as often does not detect a job that produces no output on either run. It doubles the schedule and leaves the detection problem exactly where it was.

questions.mindset: A pipeline that fails silently fails until something reports its outcome — visibility and fail-fast are the two changes that matter.

questions.scenario: An on-call engineer is using Claude Code during an outage. Their first session ended after a tool error and everything since has been slower: the same investigation restarts, earlier findings are gone, and each attempt begins from the beginning.
questions.stem: What is the MOST likely cause and the BEST response?

options.text: The session ended and the next one began with no history. Reconstruct the investigation from the runbook and any saved findings, and record what is established as you go so a further interruption is survivable.
The agent's context has filled up from the failed session, so continuing in the same chat will keep slowing down. Start a fresh chat.
The session's file state was rolled back when the tool error occurred, so the working tree is stale. Check out the latest branch and continue.
Tool errors indicate the agent has lost track of the task, so the investigation should be restarted from the beginning with a more explicit prompt.

questions.explanation: The symptom — an earlier session ending, later work starting from nothing, repeated restarts — is the signature of **losing the session, not filling it**. The response is to rebuild from the durable sources the outage process already has: the runbook, dashboards, any notes written during the first attempt. And to record findings as you go, so the second interruption costs an hour rather than the whole investigation. That is a runbook property, not a prompting one.

whyWrong.B: A full context window is a different symptom: the session keeps going but degrades. Here the session ended, and starting a fresh chat is what already happened.
whyWrong.C: A tool error does not roll back the working tree. Nothing here describes files reverting, and the engineer would see that directly.
whyWrong.D: Restarting from the beginning discards the first attempt's findings, which is the expensive part. A more explicit prompt does not recover what was never written down.

questions.mindset: When a session ends mid-investigation, the fix is durable notes and the runbook — not a better prompt.

questions.scenario: An AI-assisted pipeline writes migration scripts against a staging copy of production. Over three weeks it has produced 40 migrations, all applied successfully in staging. On the first run against production, 6 failed and 2 produced data loss that required restoring from backup.
questions.stem: What is the MOST important lesson for the operational process?

options.text: A staging environment that shares production's data characteristics would have exposed these failures before production. Verification must run somewhere that fails the way production fails, and the process needs a tested recovery path regardless.
The agent needs more careful instructions, since the scripts succeeded in staging and so the prompt was insufficient.
Forty successful staging runs is good evidence the pipeline works, so the production failures should be treated as an unusual event.
The pipeline should stop making migrations automatically and have a person write each one, since automation is where the risk comes from.

questions.explanation: Forty successes in an environment that cannot fail the way production fails is **not evidence of correctness** — it is evidence that the test did not exercise the risk. The data loss in particular usually comes from volume, character encoding or constraints that differ between staging and production. The process lesson is that the verification environment has to share the relevant characteristics, and that a tested recovery path matters as much as the check, because a check that catches a problem still leaves you mid-migration.

whyWrong.B: The scripts were correct against the environment they ran in. Instructions do not change how staging differs from production, and the failure mode here is structural rather than a wording problem.
whyWrong.C: This is the trap the question is about. Success rate in a permissive environment measures how little the environment challenged the work, and the two data-loss failures are evidence against the generalisation.
whyWrong.D: Removing automation removes the volume problem but also the throughput benefit, and it does not address the real gap — that the verification environment was not representative. A human writing the same migration would hit the same encoding difference.

questions.mindset: Verification only counts if the environment fails the way production fails — otherwise success measures how little the test challenged the work.

questions.scenario: An organisation wants a runbook for its AI-assisted pipeline covering what to do when it produces a change that breaks the build, when a pipeline step fails silently, and when a reviewer suspects a generated change was not actually reviewed.
questions.stem: Which TWO elements are MOST important in that runbook? Choose TWO.

options.text: A defined detection signal for each failure and who is accountable for it — because the failure that costs most is the one nobody is watching for.
A recovery step for each failure that can be executed without judgement about the codebase, so the first responder is not diagnosing under pressure.
The prompt used for each pipeline stage, so the runbook can be used to reproduce the change exactly.
The list of engineers who have completed training on the tooling, so the runbook knows who to contact.

questions.explanation: A runbook earns its place in the two situations that decide its value: **the alert that never comes**, and **the responder who is not the person who built the pipeline**. Naming the detection signal and its owner converts 'nobody noticed for a week' into a page. And a recovery step executable without deep codebase judgement means the response is mechanical at three in the morning, which is when it is needed. Prompts and training lists are documentation of a different kind.

whyWrong.C: The prompt explains how the pipeline was built, which is documentation rather than operations. During an incident nobody needs to reproduce the change — they need to stop the bleeding and know whether the pipeline can be trusted.
whyWrong.D: Training records belong in an onboarding tracker. During an incident the question is what to do and who is paged, not who has been through an introduction.

questions.mindset: An operations runbook needs a detection signal with an owner and a recovery step executable without deep judgement.

questions.scenario: A team has a well-tuned prompt for writing tests against their existing patterns. It works well on their own code. On a module written by a different team it produces tests that pass but assert almost nothing. A reviewer has flagged this twice.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective improvement?

options.text: Add a check on the tests themselves — require at least one assertion that fails when the function under test is broken — because a test that cannot fail verifies nothing regardless of how well it matches the local style.
Add examples of strong tests from the team's own code, so the pattern transfers to the other team's module.
Use a more capable model for this module, since generating meaningful assertions requires reasoning the current model is not doing.
Ask the other team to adopt the same test conventions, so the prompt's pattern assumptions hold everywhere.

questions.explanation: Tests that pass and assert nothing are the most dangerous output in this workflow, because **they are indistinguishable from good tests by the fact that they pass**. The check on the test itself — that it fails when the code is broken — is what distinguishes them, and it converts a plausible-looking deliverable into one that either proves something or fails visibly. The team's tuned prompt was never going to address this, because it encodes local style rather than test strength.

whyWrong.B: Examples of strong tests help with style and idiom, which is not the failure here. The other team's tests are not stylistically wrong; they assert nothing, and style guidance does not fix that.
whyWrong.C: A stronger model produces better-written tests that still assert nothing. The gap is a missing verification step on the output, not a limit on what the model can write.
whyWrong.D: Changing another team's conventions is a large, slow change to fix a test-quality gap. Requiring a failing assertion fixes it regardless of whose conventions the tests follow.

questions.mindset: A passing test proves nothing until you check it fails against broken code — that check is what makes a generated test meaningful.

questions.scenario: A 60-person platform team has been using Claude Code for eight months. Their instructions file has grown to 300 lines, contains two rules that contradict each other, names a service that was retired in June, and includes a paragraph of the original author's personal preferences about commit messages.
questions.stem: What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Triage it: keep the rules that hold for all work in the shared file, move the service-specific detail to the service's own instructions, delete what no longer applies, and resolve the two contradictions by stating which rule wins.
Move it all to organisation-wide settings, so the whole company benefits from 300 lines of accumulated guidance.
Add a line at the top saying 'follow the most specific and most recent rule', which resolves the contradictions without editing anything.
Start a new instructions file from scratch, since 300 lines accumulated over eight months cannot be recovered.

questions.explanation: This is the ordinary shape of an unmanaged instruction file, and each element has its own disposition: **the always-true rules stay shared**, the service-specific detail moves to where that service is worked on, the retired service's rules go, the author's personal preferences go with them, and the two contradictions get an explicit resolution. 'Most recent and most specific' cannot resolve two rules that are equally specific and were written at different times — which is the state described.

whyWrong.B: Pushing 300 lines including one author's commit preferences to every team in the company spreads contradictions and obsolete rules to hundreds of engineers who do not work on this service.
whyWrong.C: Recency is not authority here. Two conflicting rules written at different times would resolve in favour of the newer one regardless of which is correct, which is how a deprecated practice becomes the enforced one.
whyWrong.D: Eight months of accumulated rules contain real institutional knowledge about how this team works. Discarding it wholesale loses more than it cleans, and the contradictions and obsolete lines are a small, identifiable part.

questions.mindset: An instruction file needs triage: what is always true stays shared, what is specific moves, what is dead goes, and contradictions get an explicit resolution.

questions.scenario: A team runs Claude Code in strict mode for everyday work and unlocked permission mode only for a weekly dependency upgrade. After the upgrade, a dependency's post-install script pushed a branch to the repository's upstream remote. The branch was never merged.
questions.stem: What is the MOST important control that would have prevented this?

options.text: Keeping the permission mode strict throughout and running the upgrade's own scripts outside the agent session, so no code the agent runs can act on the repository's credentials or remotes.
A deny rule for the post-install script pattern, so the agent cannot invoke dependency install scripts directly.
A pre-merge hook that blocks branches pushed to the upstream remote without a matching pull request.
Instruction text in the project file telling the agent never to run commands that push to a remote.

questions.explanation: This is a **containment** failure, and containment is what permission modes are for: the session that ran untrusted post-install code should not have had the ability to act on the repository's credentials or push anywhere. Running installation scripts outside the agent session keeps that trust boundary intact — the script runs with a human's attention on it. Deny rules and pre-merge hooks are narrower: the first is a pattern block that a differently-named script evades, the second acts after the push has already authenticated and left.

whyWrong.B: A deny rule on the script pattern is a genuine defence but it is pattern-based, and post-install scripts vary in name and invocation across package managers. It narrows the exposure without closing the boundary that was opened.
whyWrong.C: A pre-merge hook prevents an unwanted merge, not the push. The branch exists on the remote, the credentials were used, and anything that reacts to remote events has already run.
whyWrong.D: An instruction is a request, and this is exactly the case where a request is the weakest of the four: the agent is running third-party code whose behaviour is not the agent's own intent to follow.

questions.mindset: For untrusted code, containment beats filtering — keep the session that runs third-party scripts away from the credentials and the remotes.

questions.scenario: A company wants most of its engineers to have the same approved MCP servers available in Claude Code. Security has reviewed and approved twelve. Each team needs a different subset, engineers must be able to add whichever approved server their work needs, and nothing unapproved may be installable by anyone.
questions.stem: What is the BEST configuration approach?

options.text: Set managed settings to deny MCP server addition outright, so the approved set is the only set. Teams that need more get an exception through the same review that approved the twelve.
Document the twelve approved servers in the project instructions and ask engineers to install the ones they need, since the list is authoritative once it is written down.
Let each team configure its own subset in project settings, and review the configurations quarterly.
Allow engineers to add any server on request through the normal tooling, and rely on code review to catch an unapproved one before it is used.

questions.explanation: Two requirements point in opposite directions — engineers need flexibility to add **approved** servers, and nobody may add unapproved ones — and managed settings are what resolve it, because they apply regardless of project or personal configuration. Denying server addition at that level makes the reviewed list the only list, and the review path stays open for the teams that genuinely need something new. Quarterly review of twelve configurations is a weaker control with a longer window.

whyWrong.B: Documentation creates a request, not a restriction. An engineer can add any server they like regardless of what a file lists, and the list goes stale as new servers are approved.
whyWrong.C: This leaves configuration to the teams, which is the thing the requirement forbids. Quarterly review means an unapproved server can be in place for months, and it cannot stop installation in the meantime.
whyWrong.D: Code review looks at changes, and adding an MCP server is not a change. Review is also the wrong layer for a supply-chain decision, since the server is installed before there is anything to review.

questions.mindset: When a reviewed list must be the only list, enforce it above project and personal configuration — documentation and periodic review are not controls.

questions.scenario: A team uses Claude Code in a repository where a large part of the codebase predates their conventions. Developers have found that suggestions in that area are consistently off-pattern, and the team wants the agent to follow the conventions there too.
questions.stem: Which approach is MOST likely to work, and why?

options.text: Document the conventions for that area in the instructions that apply to it, and have the agent read the surrounding code before editing — the conventions have to be stated where they apply, and the existing code is the best worked example available.
Ask the agent to read the whole repository before making any change, so it learns the conventions from the code.
Use a more capable model for that area, since the difficulty is understanding an unfamiliar legacy pattern.
Plan to rewrite that area to match the current conventions, so the inconsistency disappears.

questions.explanation: The conventions in a legacy area are **a local fact that nothing in the request carries**, and the two sources that do carry it are the instructions that apply to that area and the code next to the change. Stating them and reading the surroundings puts both in view before an edit. Reading the whole repository buries the local patterns under the volume, a stronger model has the same missing information, and rewriting is a large project being proposed to solve a prompting problem.

whyWrong.B: This puts a large amount of material in context to find a handful of local patterns, and the legacy patterns compete with the majority of the codebase that follows current conventions. The nearby code is the relevant sample.
whyWrong.C: Capability is not the missing input. The conventions are stated nowhere and are inconsistent with the rest of the repository, which is a knowledge gap rather than a reasoning one.
whyWrong.D: Rewriting a legacy area is a significant project with its own risk, and it is being proposed to solve a problem that stating the conventions addresses.

questions.mindset: Where conventions are local and inconsistent with the rest, state them where they apply and let the adjacent code be the worked example.

questions.scenario: A team uses Claude Code to add small, well-specified changes across many services. Each change is independent, the existing tests confirm correctness, and the work is latency-tolerant. Someone proposes a single long unattended session that works through the backlog.
questions.stem: What is the BEST approach, and why?

options.text: Work through the backlog as independent units, each with its own verification and its own commit, so a failure in one does not stop the rest and a reviewer can check each change on its own evidence.
Run one long session, because carrying context forward across the backlog saves the agent from re-reading each service's conventions.
Batch all the changes into one branch and one pull request, so the reviewer sees the whole set at once.
Have the agent open the pull requests without waiting for test results, since the existing tests are known to be reliable.

questions.explanation: When each unit is independent and independently verifiable, **the unit of work should be the unit of verification and the unit of review**. Independent commits mean a failure in one service does not block the rest, the tests confirm each conversion, and a reviewer can check a small change against its own test evidence rather than reasoning about forty. One long session also accumulates context and history that are not what makes the work correct — the tests are.

whyWrong.B: Context carried across forty unrelated services is not what makes each change correct; the tests are. The long session instead accumulates history, couples the changes' fate together, and makes each pull request harder to review.
whyWrong.C: One branch with forty changes makes review slower and riskier, and a single defect blocks everything. It also removes the natural point at which a problem in one service can be caught and isolated.
whyWrong.D: Opening pull requests before tests pass inverts the order in which verification has value, and known reliability is not a reason to remove the check from this particular change.

questions.mindset: When work units are independent and independently verifiable, make each one its own verification and review boundary.

questions.scenario: During a production incident an SRE wants an agent to help read logs, query metrics and inspect cluster state. They propose running it with permissions skipped so nothing blocks, relying on an incident-specific instruction file to keep it careful, and on the fact that the agent is a well-regarded internal tool.
questions.stem: What is the BEST response?

options.text: Keep the tool narrowly scoped for the incident: read-only access to what the investigation needs, write actions taken by the engineer, and a short session. Unattended write access during an incident is when an unintended change is hardest to attribute.
Proceed with permissions skipped, because an incident is the one situation where speed matters more than guardrails.
Proceed, but require the incident instruction file to be reviewed by a second engineer before the session starts.
Proceed with read-only access, but keep permissions skipped so that diagnostic commands are not blocked one by one.

questions.explanation: An incident justifies removing friction from the **investigation**, not from **change**. Reading logs, metrics and cluster state needs no write access at all, so there is no reason to grant it, and during an incident the cost of an unintended write is at its highest: the system is already fragile and attribution is hardest when several people and one agent have been changing things. Read-only plus a human taking write actions is both faster and safer.

whyWrong.B: Speed matters and this is the slowest option to establish trust in. Skipping permissions means nothing distinguishes an intended change from an unintended one, which is precisely the distinction an incident cannot afford to lose.
whyWrong.C: Reviewing the instruction file addresses whether the agent is told to be careful. It does not change what the agent is able to do, and the two have come apart every time a prompt is the only control.
whyWrong.D: Read-only access is the substance of the recommendation and 'permissions skipped' removes it. Broad permissions with read-only intent is the same configuration as the unacceptable option, described in more careful words.

questions.mindset: In an incident, remove friction from the investigation and keep change authority with the engineer — guardrails matter most when the system is fragile.
